title: The First Condition for Equilibrium
lead: Two conditions have to be met before a system is in equilibrium, and this section states the first of them: the net external force on the system must be zero, and because a force has components it must be zero along every axis at once. A motionless person meets that condition and so does a car driving at a constant velocity, which is why equilibrium is not the same as being at rest. The condition is also not enough on its own, as two equal and opposite forces applied at different places on an ice hockey stick show: the net external force is zero and the stick rotates all the same.
objectives: State the first condition of equilibrium.
summary_html:
• Statics is the study of forces in equilibrium.
  • Two conditions must be met to achieve equilibrium, which is defined to be motion without linear or rotational acceleration.
  • The first condition necessary to achieve equilibrium is that the net external force on the system must be zero, so that $\text{net}\;\mathbf{F}=0$.

figures.original_caption: This motionless person is in static equilibrium. The forces acting on him add up to zero. Both forces are vertical in this case.

This car is in dynamic equilibrium because it is moving at constant velocity. There are horizontal and vertical forces, but the net external force in any direction is zero. The applied force F_app between the tires and the road is balanced by air friction, and the weight of the car is supported by the normal forces, here shown to be equal for all four tires.

An ice hockey stick lying flat on ice with two equal and opposite horizontal forces applied to it. Friction is negligible, and the gravitational force is balanced by the support of the ice (a normal force). Thus, net F = 0. Equilibrium is achieved, which is static equilibrium in this case.

exercises.prompt: What can you say about the velocity of a moving body that is in dynamic equilibrium? Draw a sketch of such a body using clearly labeled arrows to represent all external forces on the body.

answer.solution: Its velocity is constant. That means more than a steady speed: neither the size of the velocity nor its direction changes, so the acceleration is zero and, by Newton’s second law, the net external force on the body is zero. A car rounding a bend at a steady speed is therefore not in dynamic equilibrium, because its direction is changing. For the sketch, take the car of Figure 9.3 driving along a level road. Draw an arrow forward from the tires labelled F_app for the force the road applies to them, an arrow backward of exactly the same length labelled f for the air friction, a long arrow straight down from the middle of the car labelled w for its weight, and an upward arrow at each tire labelled N whose four lengths together equal the length of w. The horizontal pair cancels and the vertical forces cancel, so the net external force is zero in every direction while the car keeps its velocity.

exercises.prompt: Under what conditions can a rotating body be in equilibrium? Give an example.

answer.solution: Equilibrium is defined as motion without linear or rotational acceleration, so a rotating body is in equilibrium when it turns at a constant rate and the net external force on it is zero as well. A steady rotation is the rotational counterpart of a constant velocity, just as dynamic equilibrium is. A wheel spinning freely on a well-oiled axle is an example: the axle carries its weight, nothing speeds the rotation up or slows it down, and the wheel turns on at the rate it was given. The ice hockey stick of Figure 9.5 is not such a case, since its rotation accelerates, and that is why the first condition alone cannot decide the question; the section that follows adds the quantity, torque, that the second condition is written in.
